title: Compare & order fractions
examples: Teacher, how do I know which fraction is bigger?
Can you show me how to use the common denominator?
Is cross-multiplying always the easiest way?

explain.say: Today we will learn to compare and order fractions. We can use a few helpful methods. First we will find a common denominator.
Now look! Here it is in 3D: fractions of a pie. Can you see the whole pie and the one slice? Tap any part, and I will tell you about it.

To find a common denominator we look for the least common multiple of the two denominators. For example we compare one half and two thirds. The denominators are two and three. The smallest number both can go into is six.
We change both fractions to have six as the bottom number. One half becomes three sixths. Two thirds becomes four sixths. Now we can compare three sixths and four sixths.
Another helpful trick is using the benchmark half. If a fraction is bigger than half it is larger. For example five ninths is bigger than half because five is more than four point five.

The third way is cross-multiplying when you cannot find a common denominator easily. We multiply the top of the first by the bottom of the second. Then we multiply the top of the second by the bottom of the first. We compare these two new numbers.

faq.q: Why do I need a common denominator?
faq.a: You need a common denominator so that the pieces are the same size. You cannot compare apples and oranges. It makes the comparison fair.
asks: What is the purpose of finding a common denominator?

faq.a: The benchmark half is the fraction one divided by two. It is a helpful reference point to see if a fraction is bigger or smaller than half.
asks: How do I use the benchmark half?
Is half always a good comparison point?

faq.a: You should use cross-multiplying when the denominators are different and finding a common multiple seems too hard. It is a reliable backup method.
asks: Is cross-multiplying always the best way?
What if the numbers are very big?

faq.q: Can I order three or more fractions?
faq.a: Yes you can. You just need to find a common denominator for all the denominators. Then you compare the numerators.
asks: How do I order four fractions?
Do I do this step by step?

faq.q: Does cross-multiplying give me the actual answer?
faq.a: No it does not give you the actual value of the fraction. It only gives you numbers to compare to see which fraction is larger.
asks: Is the cross-multiplied number the answer?
What do I do with the two products?

facts: To compare fractions, they must have the same denominator or a common multiple of denominators.
A fraction is greater than one half if its numerator is more than half of its denominator.
Cross-multiplying compares two fractions by comparing the two resulting products.
The least common multiple is the smallest number that a set of numbers can all divide into evenly.

quiz.why: We find the common denominator, which is eight. Three fourths becomes six eighths. Six eighths is larger than five eighths.

wrong.1: This is tempting because five is a larger number than three.
wrong.2: This is tempting because they both look like they are close to each other.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might not know the method yet.

quiz.why: When the denominators are the same, the fraction with the larger numerator is the larger fraction.

wrong.0: This is tempting because the numbers look similar.
wrong.1: This is tempting because you might need a different method.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might look at the top number first.

quiz.why: Cross-multiplying gives us two products. Two times seven is fourteen. Five times three is fifteen. Since fifteen is larger than fourteen, five sevenths is larger.

wrong.0: This is tempting because two is smaller than five.
wrong.1: This is tempting because they are both fractions.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you cannot see the answer right away.
